expert.item: Leveled compaction minimizes space amplification at the cost of read and write amplification — it keeps one sorted run per level, merging aggressively.

Tiered compaction (RocksDB's own 'Universal' style) trades the other way: write amplification is usually lower than leveled's, at the cost of higher read and space amplification, since more sorted runs coexist before merging.
FIFO compaction does no merging at all: it drops the oldest file once the total size is exceeded, for cache-like data where recency, not correctness of old data, is all that matters.
Read, write and space amplification are each precisely defined as a ratio (actual data moved or stored, divided by the logical amount), with a theoretical minimum of 1.0 for each.
The RUM conjecture: an access method optimal in one of read, update (write) and memory (space) overhead cannot be optimal in both of the other two at once.

A write stall has two concrete, named triggers in RocksDB: too many L0 files (slowdown then stop thresholds) and too many pending-compaction bytes (soft then hard thresholds) — both because compaction has fallen behind the write rate.

Without write stalls, a write rate compaction can't keep up with grows space amplification without bound (risking running out of disk) and read amplification without bound (every read must check more and more uncompacted structures).

Compaction debt is the backlog of merge work a storage engine owes itself; it is the real-world shape the RUM conjecture takes for an LSM tree, since choosing less write amplification now (less compaction) means paying more read and space amplification later, until that debt is paid down.
expert.source: self (synthesis of RUM paper + RocksDB Compaction/Write Stalls)

expert.item: Tombstone build-up (taught directly in the previous topic) is the same debt in miniature: a tombstone is uncollected compaction work, and it is compaction, not a flush or a read, that finally discards it.

Whether a B-tree or an LSM tree wins is a workload question, not a universal ranking: it depends on the actual read/write/space amplification measured for a given workload, which this chapter's own lab measures directly rather than citing received wisdom.
expert.source: RUM Conjecture paper (complexity table, B+-Tree vs. Levelled LSM) + examples.py

expert.item: Cassandra, ScyllaDB and Pebble each default to a different point on the same leveled/tiered spectrum RocksDB exposes as configuration — named as reference points for where real systems sit, not measured directly in this sandbox.

at.out: named only, not measured; this topic measures RocksDB and Postgres directly rather than running three more engines
